utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. I see Mr. Josse absent, Mr. Bourgon, as he had indicated yesterday and the rest are -- seem to be present, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye for the Prosecution. All right. Just before we continue, I just wanted to make an announcement. On the 27th of April, we were scheduled to sit in the afternoon. We have succeeded in moving it to the morning, all right? And there is also another day in May where we are trying to do the same but since it's not yet confirmed, I will confirm it in due course. Thank you. Good morning to you, Mr. Ristic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I hope you had a good rest. Today we will continue with the cross-examination, with your testimony and hopefully finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Haynes will take over and Mr. Bourgon will continue after he returns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I think also Mr. Meek may have a few questions of this witness but other than that, I don't think any of the accused propose to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ristic.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that you know who I am, I'm counsel for Vinko Pandurevic and I will be asking questions on his behalf. I hope, if you won't mind, if I begin with a few personal questions. Would you mind telling us how old you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And are you a married man?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Grbavci, near Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And have you lived there all your life?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Prior to the war, was that a Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village has about 40 households, Donji Grbavci consists of Serbian households and then around that village there are also Muslim villages or more hamlets. I would rather call them hamlets. And they had mixed population, both Muslim and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if you could just briefly tell us what military experience you had had before the start of the war in Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no military experience whatsoever before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But when the war started, it's right, as you told us yesterday, that you became the platoon commander for the TO in your village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were the villages in the area of Bosnia in which you lived defended in precisely the same way at the start of the war, by the formation of TOs from the local population?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, both Serbian and Muslim population kept guard, each protecting their own village. Later on, in 1992, at the initiative of the Crisis Staff, we organised platoons and companies in villages consisting of men who were fit for military service. They selected commanders for platoons and companies. In my village we had a platoon because it was a small village and I only had 25 men fit for military service when we first went to the positions in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were the Serbian defence forces linked in any way at the start of the war or were they, as it were, separated by intervening Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, these forces operated only in villages and then in June when we went to positions, it was already separate. We had our positions at Parlog. We went to the positions on the 11th of June in the evening and we remained there throughout the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think as you told us yesterday, throughout the entire time, up until the 15th of July of 1995, you had no combat experience at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want briefly to deal with your commanding officer, Pero [Realtime transcript read in error "pf"] Vidakovic. Was he somebody who, prior to the war, had had any experience as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no experience whatsoever, just like I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, can you repeat his first name, please, again, because it didn't show up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It might be easier if the witness said it because he will get it right and I probably won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you just give us the name of your commanding officer, please, Mr. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Vidakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1992, the Zvornik Brigade was formed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And from that time until the arrival of Vinko Pandurevic as its commander it had a number of different commanders, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think in total five, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And although a brigade was formed, its composition was still the same people who had comprised the TOs prior to that time, the -- in your area, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All companies which existed were companies from villages. They were on the positions, and they were there during that period of time, before Pandurevic arrived. People changed, some came, some went, but the essence remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so the 4th Battalion which covered the area in which you were born and brought up was commanded by a man with no military experience and comprised substantially of non-professional, non-full-time soldiers, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In our battalion, a lot of commanders succeeded each other, Commander Vidakovic was either the 7th or the 8th commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the purpose of the formation of the Zvornik Brigade was to defend the Serbian-occupied territory that had been established by June 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in particular, and we'll come to have a look at it in a minute, your battalion, the 4th Battalion, had a defence line which it was responsible for?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to look at, with you, please, the strength of the Zvornik Brigade in terms of numbers and military hardware. And I wonder if to that end, we could have in e-court, please, P00382 at page 2 in the B/C/S and the English, please. In fact, given that it's just a list, we probably only need to look at it in one language so we'll stay with the B/C/S, please. If you look down that list, hold it there, please, you will see the manning strength of the respective battalions of the Zvornik Brigade, and this is a document that's dated the 20th of July of 1995, and if the document could be moved just slightly to the left, you will see, Mr. Ristic, that the numbers of the 4th Battalion are said to be 543. Would that be about right, according to your understanding of the strength of the battalion in July of 1995? I think for the witness the document needs to go a little bit to the left.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's most likely an accurate piece of information. Yesterday I said 450 but 543 is probably an accurate figure. It's been a long time so I forgot and I never had the exact data on our strength. There were a lot of people who were listed as members of the battalion but were on sick leave or something like that, but yes, this figure must be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if the document could be just brought up a little bit and to the left, the total number of men available to the Zvornik Brigade, I mean down rather than up, available to the Zvornik Brigade in July of 1995 was 5010 according to this document. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's most likely correct. I know that there were about 5.000 but as for the exact figure, yes, this seems like an accurate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could just be patient with us a little bit longer, Mr. Ristic, I'm going to ask you to look at another document and that's P00381, at page 4 in the English, or page 3 in the B/C/S. Again it's a list and it probably doesn't need to be in both languages. Given that it's in B/C/S, I wonder if you could just confirm for us that what we see on this page, and again it's a document from July of 1995, is a spreadsheet setting out the weapons available to the Zvornik Brigade. Would you agree with that? Perhaps we could go back up to the top of the page. Mr. Ristic, you agree that that shows us the weaponry available to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. This was the weaponry. I don't have the exact figures as to the weaponry. This is official information and, yes, we did have these weapons in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And perhaps it might be an idea so that the English speakers understand it if we now look at it in English so we can see what those weapons were. In the English it's page 4. Thank you very much, Madam Usher. And so, for example, we can see that there were over 2.000 semi-automatic rifles available, nearly 2.000 automatic rifles, rocket launchers, anti-aircraft machine-guns, mortars, Howitzers, self-propelled guns, rocket launchers and the like. That was the range of weaponry available to the Zvornik Brigade in July of 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on. You told us yesterday that on the 1st of July you were present at a meeting at Zvornik Brigade command at which Vinko Pandurevic announced he was taking a force to Srebrenica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in fact, your battalion contributed some men to that force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware of the size of the force that was taken from the Zvornik Brigade to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe it was discussed but I can't remember that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and jog your memory. Do you recall that it was a battalion plus additional logistical support that was taken to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would roughly be the case, the size of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And a battalion was about 500 men, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we are clear, remaining behind in Zvornik, therefore, were about 4 and a half thousand soldiers plus most of the weaponry that we've seen on the documents we've just been looking at?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was a perfectly adequate force to defend the lines that the Zvornik Brigade was designed to control, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on from that, please, if I may, and just discuss with you briefly the period of time you spent working as a deputy security commander in the 4th Battalion. Can you just remind us what period it was that you were served as a deputy security commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From March 1993, for roughly two years, probably until May of 1995, when I moved to the establishment position of assistant battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ristic. And just to summarise what you told us yesterday, effectively, there were two areas of your work as a security commander. One was external security, which was, as it were, intelligence about the enemy, and the other was internal security that involved investigations into members of your own forces. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as part of your work as a deputy security commander, you had regular meetings with the brigade security commander, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not sure you told us this but how regular would they be? Weekly, monthly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never determined. It was upon invitation by the chief of brigade, but this was not on any regular terms. It was upon invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at these meetings with the brigade security commander, were the security commanders or deputy commanders from the other battalions also present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that my learned friend is referring accurately to the role of the head of security as a commander. I wondered if we could just clarify that for the record. I believe that he's using it in a colloquial sense in terms of referring to the head of the unit or the organ but I just want the record to be clear as to -- because "commander" has certain military connotations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the title of your position in the battalion between March 1993 and May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From March 1993 to March 1995, is this what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, before he said May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I said May 1995 as well in my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were telling me the role you fulfilled as a security officer. I want you to tell me what the title of your office was as you understood it to be.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander for security of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who was your direct line superior? And what was his title?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander was the supreme superior in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was your direct superior in terms of the security branch of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nobody else in the battalion, which means that my superior in the battalion was my commander, and deputy commander by establishment. They were above me. I received my orders from them and I cooperated with the assistant commander for security in the brigade. The chief of security in the brigade, that is. I was subordinate to my commander and this was my position in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just so we're clear, who was chief of--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was chief of security in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic was the chief of security in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was it with him that you held or that you attended regular meetings of security officers?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you understand Drago Nikolic's title to be?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of security in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, now we've made that ten-minute diversion, I hope the Prosecution is satisfied. Now, at these regular meetings, did you discuss matters relating to investigations into members of your own battalion and other soldiers in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they did in the brigade when it came to these issues. I know that there were no investigations in the battalion. The security in the organ in the battalion could talk to the soldiers and this is what was done to the soldiers who caused problems or had problems, and then in consultation with the brigade, which had its legal office, they had their legal officers, we asked for their assistance. Our soldiers would receive assistance on this -- these matters from the legal officers and the chief of security, but we are talking minor disciplinary matters only, those were just minor problems, absence from duty or things like that, nothing major.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of your line of reporting, when it came to investigations into internal security, to whom would you report?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that happened in the battalion regarding these matters would be communicated to the commander by the assistant commander for security if it did not concern the commander himself. He knew everything. He had authority to punish a soldier with up to seven days imprisonment if this soldier committed a disciplinary offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you ever a party to investigations that concerned a commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you like this, Mr. Haynes, but I think we need to make this clear. When on page 10 at lines 11 to 14, in response to Mr. Vanderpuye's intervention, you asked the witness to explain exactly his title, his position and title, he described himself as the assistant commander for security. Then very rightly so, when, in lines 22, 23, he said, at least according to the transcript, "I cooperated with the assistant commander for security in the brigade," which would be himself, then there was this clarification that that means the chief of security in the brigade, and he explained to us who that is. Now, if we come back to your last question and his last answer, or the previous -- the penultimate one, he says, "Everything that happened in the battalion regarding these matters would be communicated to the commander by the assistant commander for security, if it did not concern the commander himself." Who would be the assistant commander for security in this case? Would it be himself or would it be what was previously referred to as the chief of security? I'm referring specifically to page 12, lines 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if the witness followed that. I'm going to see if I can ask a couple of questions to clear it up for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it needs to be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a hypothetical situation because you've told us it never occurred in your experience, but if there was an investigation which involved the commander of a battalion, as I understand the position, that would not be communicated to the commander of the battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In case the battalion commander was involved in making certain mistakes that would jeopardise the security of the soldiers, then the assistant commander in the battalion could report to the chief of security in the brigade of what had happened, in which case this person, in agreement with the commander of the brigade or the chief of brigade, would call this person and based on the information that he had received from the assistant commander for security, they would carry out investigation, if this commander had jeopardised the position and the work of the battalion. If -- I -- I wanted to say that I was the assistant commander in the battalion for security. This is something that I might have omitted when I spoke about my title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in a case where the investigation involved a soldier other than the commander, the investigations of the security organ would be communicated to the battalion commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who would communicate the result of your investigations to the battalion commander? Would that be you or would that be a brigade officer for security?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander of battalion for security would be the first to report to his commander about those events because this concerned a soldier from our battalion and if we were not able to resolve the issue and deal with the problem, then we would go to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that's cleared it up. If it hasn't, I'll accept any guidance as to where I can go from here but other than that, I'm going to leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can proceed. It's clear enough. But in order to help us, since you were an assistant commander for security in the battalion, and it seems to have been also an assistant commander for security in the brigade, try to keep that distinction in mind as you proceed so that responsibilities are kept distinct and clear. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the brigade, the title was chief of security, and in the battalion, it was the assistant commander for security. This is the difference. In the brigade, the chief was subordinated to the brigade commander, and the case was the same in the battalion. That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's very clear now. Mr. Haynes, again my apologies for the interruption but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think it was quite justified, Your Honour. There were a lot of confusing terms flying around at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to move on now and deal with your role as deputy commander of the battalion, if I may. You dealt with this a lot yesterday so I'm not going to go over the same ground but I want to just ask you how it was that you received orders as a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from the brigade? From the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's a separate question I'm going to move on to, from whom you could receive orders. I'm really asking the medium by which you received orders. Did you receive orders in writing?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it yesterday. The orders that came from the brigade arrived either directly via the telephone, looking for somebody from the command, if the commander was there they would be looking for him first. But a lot of the orders also came through the communications officers who received the order from their counterparts in the brigade and then they would forward the order to the -- to a member of the command, the commander himself or any other member of the command who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that's how you would receive orders from the brigade. Was there any other source from which you could receive orders as a battalion commander or deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received orders from the battalion commander, and I also received orders when he wasn't there, when he was absent, I received orders from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it possible that you would receive orders from a superior officer at corps, at the corps command?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible, probably, but I did not have an opportunity to receive any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And going back to what we were discussing earlier, as a security commander, could you receive orders from somebody other than, as it were, your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to receive orders from anybody else. I never received orders from the security organs in the brigade. We had meetings. That's how we worked. I don't remember ever having received an order or ever having a possibility to receive an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Receiving orders from the brigade would necessarily have involved you receiving orders from Vinko Pandurevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Vinko Pandurevic was in the brigade, he would issue orders to us. If he was absent, there was a chief who was responsible, who would issue orders, and there were also others but in any case, the work in the battalion boiled down to the work with the duty officer, if the commander, the chief, were absent. We had received communication about all events through the duty officer in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In terms of the orders you received from Vinko Pandurevic, did you ever receive from him an order to do anything illegal or criminal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think there is perhaps some confusion with respect to the capacity in which these orders were or might have been received from the brigade commander. The witness has testified in terms of his occupation in three capacities, one was as the assistant commander for security within the battalion, the other was as the deputy commander of the battalion, and finally he had testified in terms of standing in for the commander of the battalion. It's not clear in the context of the question in which capacity the witness would have or could have received these orders from the brigade commander and the distinction between those capacities has certain implications in terms of the authority or the command authority of the position which is being referred to and the possibility to receive orders directly from the brigade command. So I just wondered if my colleague could be more precise in framing the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can't even begin to understand what that objection is. I'm going to move on and Mr. Vanderpuye can tidy it up in re-examination if he can make what he's saying clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough because basically if you cut it down into pieces what he's been saying in these last -- he's explaining that he did not receive orders from this one or that one or -- and he points to Vinko Pandurevic as the one he would receive orders from when he was there. Otherwise, from the duty officer, et cetera, et cetera so I think it's clear enough for the time being anyway. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The last question I asked you was whether Vinko Pandurevic had ever issued you with a command to do anything criminal or illegal. Could you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never issued any such order to me. All his orders were in military terms based on the defence of the territory and the area of responsibility that we were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were his orders logical and straightforward to carry out?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever refuse to carry out any order that Vinko Pandurevic issued?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever, as it were, yourself, decide not to or to stop carrying out an order that he had issued to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it all depended on the situation. On what was going on at any given moment. Sometimes we had to make independent decisions in the battalion. It depended on the situation. If we had not received any explanation from the brigade, if the commander was not there, we had to deal with the issues very fast, but this was in the case of an attack or defence and the work in the battalion. In other words, we could do things unbeknownst to the commander but then we had to subsequently report to the commander as to what had happened while he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you've really pre-empted my next question which was when you received orders from the brigade command you had, didn't you, an obligation to report on performance of those orders?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to move on now, please, to the battalion's area of defence and I'd like you please to have a look at a map which is our 3D94 in e-court. Now, can you see that, Mr. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you read the names of the towns and villages upon it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we are going to have to go back to the map in its original form so that we can see everything on it. I'm going to ask now that the usher please gives you probably pens in two different colours, if that's possible. Now, taking one of those pens and I don't care which colour it is, I'd like you if you would to mark the position of the defence line of the 4th Battalion in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like you now, if you would, please, to mark the position of the forward command post, the EKM [sic].

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] It was in the middle of the zone of responsibility, of the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you mark, please, the depth, as it were, of the defence zone which I believe is Planinci village?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] I can't remember of the order by the battalion commander. It is well defined in depth of the territory but I've forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I'd like you now, if you would, to take up the other coloured pen and put some other markings on this map for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's identify the ones that he has marked already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you put next to the line, "Defence line"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What would you like him to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: DL, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. DL, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next is the EKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you put EKM next to where you've marked the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And one more thing I'd like you to mark on there, if you would. Would you mark the position of the units for the rear and the support?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will first mark the command post that was in Rebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you put CP against that mark, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then the rear -- units for the rear and support, Planinci, you could put RS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The unit for logistical support for the battalion was near the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of the rear now. When you put that marking near Planinci, what were you referring to, between Planinci and Orahovac. What's that supposed to indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area in depth of territory, in case of an attack, the soldiers from the front end were supposed to withdraw into this sector. That's what I was referring to, because that was in the order of the battalion commander. It was specified what was the reserve positions if the line had to be pulled back, the defence line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So how shall we mark that, DT? D for delta, T for tango.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And would you put a special marking for what Mr. Haynes has indicated units for the rear and for the support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks] LP for logistical support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you can move to other markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Before we do I just want to clear up the position. The 4th Battalion had an area of responsibility or an area of defence that covered the defence line, the command post, the forward command post, and the areas around the markings you've made in the top left-hand corner of the map, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the marking you've made above Planinci is a notional line to which you were to withdraw in the event you had to abandon the defence lines, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to be absolutely clear, Orahovac was not within your area of defence at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to take up a pen of a different colour now, if you could. Have you got a different coloured pen? And I'd like you to mark for me now three things. Firstly, I'd like you to mark the line which the column of Muslims took moving towards you from the rear of your defence line.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you just put a C by the side of that blue line?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: C for Charlie and for column, thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like you now to mark, again in blue, if you would, firstly the position where you saw the flag that you referred to yesterday, and secondly the position where you saw the fire that you referred to yesterday. And it might be useful if you drew a flag and perhaps for the fire drew an asterisk or a star.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I'm just going to ask you a couple more questions on the map before I get you to initial it and we preserve it. From Zvornik to the forward command post of the brigade, there are a number of ways of travelling. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: One way would be to take the road which runs from east to west across the bottom of the plan, which is the road to Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then you would travel north past Orahovac and get to the forward command post of the brigade at Delici?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly one other way of going to Delici from the command at Karakaj would be to travel up over Jardan which we see to the extreme east of the plan. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This other road that leads to Delici, without going via Orahovac, is via Jardan, Cirjak [phon] -- Jardan, Ciraci, Kitovnice, Delici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, don't you think it would be very useful if the witness delineates for us, indicates on the map, the two routes? And perhaps just for confirming that at least I'm right in my mind, these are the two roads or routes that Mr. Sarapa wanted us to see and we saw during the site visit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was merely trying to put into the transcript that which I know you've experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be extremely useful for everyone if the witness indicates on the map the two different routes or routes as some of you would say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm always open to helpful suggestions and if the witness has understood those exchanges, perhaps he could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also because on the map some of the names that he's mentioned do not show up. So it will -- or at least I'm not seeing them so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you first, therefore, I don't know if we can come up with a third coloured pen. We can, thank you. When you've been given a third coloured pen, would you just show in perhaps dotted lines the route from Zvornik to Delici using the road to Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is what you've drawn there the route going over Jardan?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the road going via Orahovac. Orahovac, Kitovnice, Delici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you now draw the route going over Jardan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could use another colour then -- no. So I think he can use red.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or he could use dots or arrows or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And to be precise, and we were on site, Mr. Sarapa, the intersection that you indicated to us is the intersection between -- from direction of Orahovac to Hodzici. Would that be correct? In other words, that arrow which is at 9.00 in respect of Hodzici? All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa confirms that. I'm sure we can deal with that in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to have it clear this my mind, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now we are going to preserve this which is going to involve you placing some initials on that page. I would suggest in the bottom left-hand corner, since it's the least cluttered area, and it doesn't matter what colour you do that in and would you place the date on it as well?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And could that now be preserved? Yes? Now, I want to just conclude this topic. Your understanding of the position is this, isn't it, that the battalion had, under military rules, a zone of defence for which it was responsible?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you understand that in military terminology, the difference between a zone and a region is the number of points which define it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that the area which the battalion was responsible for was defined by three points: Its left, its right and its rear?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And those are the three points that you have marked on this map for us; the left and the right of the defence line and the rear where the rear services were?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was the area or the "rejon," the word is in B/C/S, for which the 4th Battalion was responsible?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, sorry to interrupt you but I don't think I did follow, or I followed in full, the difference between the zone and region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's my mistake because I used the wrong term and I will clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A battalion has an area or a rejon of defence, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And a rejon or an area is defined by three points?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military man, so it's a bit difficult for me to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the proposition I'm next going to put to you is that the smallest unit of an army which has a zone for which it is responsible is a brigade, and a zone is defined by four points. Do you understand or know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do object to my learned friend's question. I don't think that he's laid a sufficient foundation as a basis of knowledge to put the question to the witness, particularly given the most recent response of the witness indicating he's not a military man. It's difficult for him to explain these concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was only trying to answer the query of Judge Kwon as to what case I was putting, if I'm going to be stopped from doing that then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Haynes, if he can answer the question, he will answer it. If he doesn't, then he can assist us by indicating on the map the battalion's area of responsibility and the brigade's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you understand that a brigade has a zone for which it is responsible, which is defined by four points or do you not understand that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the notion of the area of responsibility of a brigade. I know the parts of the area of responsibility. However, to mark that on a map, the area of responsibility of a brigade, I couldn't do that. I could only do it for my battalion because otherwise I might make a mistake. I didn't really tour the entire area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to finish this topic, just by asking you this: Do you understand that a battalion has a rejon for which it is responsible and a brigade has a zone for which it is responsible and that those are two different concepts?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade had an area of responsibility that was the front end of the defence of the brigade, and the battalion had an area of responsibility, the front end. All battalions had their headquarters and logistical support and so did the brigade, and that was the area of responsibility, the front end of defence, both in the case of the battalion and the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to leave it there. This is something we can take up with other witnesses. Now, one last thing on this topic, although, as you've told us, Orahovac was not within your rejon, region of defence responsibility, a number of your men lived and had families that were in Orahovac in July of 1995, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And those men became concerned when they heard stories about large numbers of Muslims in the villages, in the village where their families lived, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And their concern, and the threat that that created that they might abandon their positions, created a military burden for you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It jeopardised your ability to maintain your defence line facing the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to deal with one more topic and then you'll be glad to hear, Mr. Ristic, I think we will be able to have a break. Can we be clear? Whatever Gojko Simic may or may not have done on the 14th of July, he didn't do it pursuant to any order given by you, did he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he was not in the battalion. He was on leave, at home. And he had no tasks issued to him by the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You had two names put to you yesterday. Do you remember, the names Vojo and Risto? Did you recognise the names that were put to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes, if this pertains to the two men from that village. I would say that's correct, if they were members from Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so far as you are aware, were either Vojo or Risto on duty on the 14th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be expected to know the duties or the post of each soldier in the battalion. The line of defence of the battalion consisted of two or three various sectors, and I don't know the exact tasks of each member of the battalion. However, these people were members of the 2nd Company of the 4th Battalion, together with other people from Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, are you aware whether they were people who were on leave similar to that of Gojko Simic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Who else was on leave in addition to Gojko Simic? There were nine of them. I know for a fact about Gojko Simic being on leave because I attended the party at his house. He is a relative of my wife so I attended the party. That's why I know that he was on leave. As for the other people, I don't know their names because the figure that I gave you pertained to the entire battalion, people from the entire battalion who were on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. But so that we are clear, if it were suggested that those two men, Vojo and Risto, were engaged in illegal or criminal acts on the 14th of July, did you order them to do that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't order them to do that, nor did I hear later that they participated in these acts. I definitely did not order them to do that. They had their tasks within the battalion. Now as to exact position where each soldier of the battalion was, I wasn't able to monitor all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristic. I've concluded that topic and that probably takes us to our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we go to we have the break, yesterday, you couldn't remember with precision the date of Gojko Simic's death. Do you think you can remember it today? When did he die or when was he killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I help with that after the break? I propose to put his death certificate into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, I'm going to do my best to conclude my questions for you in the next half an hour or 45 minutes. And I know it's tiring for you but, please, listen carefully and answer truthfully and as accurately as you can the remaining questions. Just to complete an inquiry made by His Honour, I wonder whether we could have put into e-court P00348 and while we are waiting for that, do you recall that you in fact signed the death certificate for Gojko Simic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when it appears, you'll be able to help us as to the date on which you did that. I think we can already see that Gojko Simic died on the 16th of July 1995, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He died on the 16th of July 1995. This is when he was found dead, but the fighting started on the 15th in the evening until the 16th in the afternoon. But he was actually found on the 17th of July when the line had been established. On the 17th we located all the fallen soldiers and Gojko Simic was among them. Most probably he got killed on the 16th as it is indicated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to come back later on to the question of members of your battalion who died but we'll leave that there. I want to move on now to the question of the column and I want to start by asking you some questions about the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Haynes, the reason why I had asked him whether he could today perhaps remember the exact date of Gojko Simic's death or killing was because at least on the 14th of July, according to his evidence, Gojko Simic was on break -- was on leave at home. What I want to know is whether, on the day that he was killed, that is apparently two days later, the 16th of July, he was still on leave or whether he had resumed his duties in the battalion. That was the reason why I had put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry and I'm sure that the witness understands the question you wish to be answered and can deal with it without any further intervention from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These soldiers were on leave from the 15th -- from the 1st to the 15th. On the 14th, they sent their sons off to the army and on the 15th they were supposed to be back to their companies and to report to the company commanders. On the 15th, the attack on the command started on the front lines of the defence. This was very early in the morning. Around 9.00 in the morning, certain men arrived at the command because the road which leaded to the companies passed by the command and they could not proceed because of the shelling. It so happened that some of them remained there. Some of them did rejoin their companies, but the fact of the matter was that on the 15th, they were supposed to report to their company commanders. I suppose that Gojko did arrive on the 15th but he could not rejoin his company because of the fighting and that's why he stayed with the command and that's where he got killed, on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 14th of July, the position was this, wasn't it? You were in command of the 4th Battalion because your commander was absent?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your brigade commander, Vinko Pandurevic, was also absent, to your knowledge, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And throughout the 14th of July, as I understand your evidence, you were virtually out of contact with Dragan Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff who was then commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And not to put too fine a point on it, this was -- you were facing what was potentially your first combat activity, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you feel you'd been abandoned by Dragan Obrenovic in a very difficult situation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the 14th? The 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think that he had abandoned me, that he had left me out in the cold. I thought that he had other things to do, that he had to intercept the column or escort a column. However, I had not received any explanation of the situation as it was on the 14th. We didn't know what this was all about. We didn't know what the situation was. But we were not even interested in that in the battalion. The situation was what it was. The battalion was at risk and the brigade command and the commanders should have helped us, should have been there. I believe that he had his duties, his tasks, for the day, and there was no need for him to think about my battalion since they had not crossed Crni Vrh yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The phrase you used yesterday was that on the 14th of July, you believed that the battalion was in grave danger. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was only in the evening, on the 14th of July, when I had received information that they were crossing Crni Vrh and that Major Obrenovic could not stop them or return them, and that evening we had received information that they were crossing Krizevacke Njive, Baljkovica on their way to Nezuk. Obviously that evening, the situation was alarming for us and we had to do something. And it was on that evening that Major Obrenovic did not communicate to us directly. We received information through the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I wonder whether therefore you could just quickly look at 7D159 to confirm that this is the information you received. And can you see between 1913 hours and 2000 hours, there is a reference here in the duty officer's notebook of the Zvornik Brigade to a communication from Premijer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that the telegram was sent at 1930 but it doesn't say who it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you need to look a little lower than that. There is an entry in the notebook beginning with the word "premijer". It may well be that you need the page moved across a little bit to the left. In the English it reads, "Inform the corps that huge columns are coming in our direction, 2000 hours." And then there is a reference to the 4th Brigade, tank firing from Boreslinovac [phoen]. Is that the information that you received on the evening of the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a different piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I'm not going to go into that any further. The fact of the matter is that on the 14th of July, your battalion was not involved in any combat activity at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that the first combat activity occurred at 4.30 in the morning on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that took the form of a heavy artillery attack on your front from the 2nd Corps of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The infantry attack was launched on the link between the 4th and the 6th Battalions and they opened artillery fire on the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did that attack last for about an hour?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack started that morning and lasted with some interruptions throughout the entire day and throughout the next day, up to the noon of the following day, up to 12.00 approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like you please now to look at another entry in the duty officer's notebook. It's 7D166. And it's a report from you at 1.30 on the afternoon of the 15th of July. It's already there in the B/C/S. You are referred to as Lazo. That's a name you're known by, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At 1.30 on the 15th of July, you had already endured a heavy attack from -- on your front, both artillery and infantry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had two fallen soldiers and several wounded, up to 1330 or 1400 hours, and up to the moment when Major Obrenovic arrived, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But at 1.30 you were able to report that everything was okay at your end. Is that a correct assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This probably meant that the line was stable. This was recorded very shortly and this meant that the line was stable more or less. This is what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. At about that time, 1.30, were you aware that Vinko Pandurevic was back at command in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first become aware on the 15th of July that Vinko Pandurevic was back in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke on the 15th of July, sometime late in the afternoon, when I spoke to my commander, the commander of the mortar platoon, Commander Pandurevic called us from the forward command post, he told me that he had arrived, and that he had sent my intervention platoon to assist me via the 7th Battalion to the Gavrici sector and that another platoon had arrived with them. They were known as the Wolves from the Drina. This -- that was the first time he ever contacted me on that day and that's when I knew that he had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you help us as to about what time that was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of the time because I did not consult my watch but I believe that it was late in the afternoon. It was already dusk and the commander of the mortar platoon asked to be allowed to change the position. He did not feel safe because the 3rd Platoon of the Infantry Battalion on the previous day had left that position and when Commander Pandurevic contacted me, he told me that he would help deal with that part of the issue and that's when I learned that the military police had arrived to assist with providing security to the mortar platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristic. You've led me nicely to the next question I want to ask you, which is about the reinforcements which were sent to help you on the 15th and going into the 16th of July. And I wonder if I put them to you whether you could simply say whether you agree that these reinforcements arrived or not. Two platoons arrived from the Bratunac Brigade, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There were some units which arrived from the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade to reinforce you, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived when Major Obrenovic arrived. One platoon of the 2nd Infantry Battalion arrived and Major Obrenovic deployed them above the command in the direction of Potocari, and he told me that one company or two platoons were from Bratunac and he also deployed them in that sector above the command in the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you've just referred to this. There were some units from the Drina Wolves which arrived to reinforce you as well, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When their commander arrived, together with Obrenovic, he brought several of his troops, I don't know whether they were just his escorts or what, and one platoon that I did not see but the commander told me, Pandurevic told me, that they had arrived together with our intervention platoon and that they were deployed on our defence line in the area of Gavrici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly another unit you've referred to a platoon of MUP policemen arrived to reinforce your forces, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th, two commanders arrived in the command. They were police commanders and they were with us. And that police was civilian police. They were somewhere on the link between the 4th and 6th Battalions. This is where I found them when we were leaving our command post on the 16th. There were some other men up there on Parlog. I don't know how many of them. There were a lot of them. They were sitting there and probably waiting for some order to arrive. They were sitting in groups of tents on the road leading from Parlog to Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the afternoon of the 15th of July, were you aware that Vinko Pandurevic was in radio communication with a commander of Muslim forces named Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having heard that on the 15th but on the 16th I am sure that I heard a conversation between our commander, Pandurevic, and Semso Muminovic about a cease-fire and about the column to be let through. I don't remember having heard any such thing on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you able to monitor the conversations between them in the sense that were you receiving reports of them through your signalman or were you able to hear them yourself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signalman could not follow anything like that but we heard it over the Motorola that was in the possession of the commander of the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm just going to see if I can help you with your memory by asking you to look at a document. It's in e-court. It's P02232, in English, page 13 and P002231, B/C/S page 17. Could the English page be moved to page 13, please? It's on page 1 at the moment. Now, Mr. Ristic, if nobody minds I'm going to explain to you what this document is because I don't expect you've ever seen it before. This is a book or a page from a book in which opposition forces intelligence recorded radio communications between your soldiers, and I want you to look, please, for an entry which is about one-third of the way down in the B/C/S, which begins, "Vuk, Lovac," can you see that, "Vuk, Lovac, 1330 hours." And it then says, "I talked to Semso (Zuko) and he wants to negotiate, he wants me to give him the frequency of the Turk who is leading the group." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you read down the next entry, "Vuk spoke to Zuko again and agreed the cease-fire under the pretense that they would negotiate later. Then he fired one more round, one for one." Now, according to the Muslim radio operators who were monitoring your conversations, those were conversations that took place on the 15th of July at about half past 1.00 and again at about quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon. Were you aware of communications between your side and Semso Muminovic at about half past 1.00 or quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another document now, please, if I may, as to the question of a cease-fire on the 15th of July. And it's 7D363, and I'll need page 3 in the B/C/S, please. This document at the moment only has an unrevised translation so I'm not going to put that on to the screen. I'm going to get the witness to read the document in B/C/S. Now, on the screen at the moment, about one, two, three, four, five, six lines up from the bottom, can you count them, Mr. Ristic? Now we've moved it. It's now -- can you see the sentence that begins, "Zavrijeni" [phoen]? Let me take it another way. There is a word there that's marked with a little square bracket. Can you see that, "dalasko" [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you count about six lines down from there, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there is a sentence that begins, "zavrijeni" [phoen]? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I wonder whether we could revert to the previous form because we've lost some of the line there. Right. Now I'm going to ask you to do us all a big favour now, Mr. Ristic. Would you read out loud the remainder of the paragraph beginning "zavrijeni" [phoen] but read it quite slowly so that the translators can translate it for us all.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the time spent at the positions at Crni Vrh, I observed movement and regrouping of a number of Muslim units, and I think that it involved several hundred of their soldiers who were in front of our line, but our orders were not to open fire on them. Thus, I suppose that this part was left as a passage for those units, in the direction of Tuzla, and that it was the initiative of the command of the VRS, to Tuzla or, rather, to the territory under the control of Muslim forces." Should I read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. That's fine. Just to place this into context for you, this is a witness statement of a man called Predrag Ilic who was one of the soldiers who was sent from Bratunac to help reinforce your lines. Do you recall yourself giving him any orders not to fire on Muslim forces in the column near Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give any orders to them whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who would have had the authority to give orders to those platoons from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were brought by Major Obrenovic, and he issued order to them, but as far as I know they spent one night there and then most likely during the night they abandoned the positions. Now as to whether somebody ordered them to do that or they did it on their own, I don't know, and they went in the direction of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to complete this, at about 2.00 on the afternoon of the 15th of July, do I understand it that you were not aware of a proposed cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of a proposed cease-fire. However, on the 16th, sometime around 10 or 11.00 most likely, I know this because after about an hour, we had to leave the command post, a man surrendered to us, he was from one of the brigades in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't mean to interrupt you but I'm going to come on to the 16th in a little while. I want to stay, if I can, for the moment on the 15th and I'd like you now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, just before you do so, just for the record, in page -- on page 37, lines 16 -- 17, sorry and 19, we have Potocari there. We obviously mean to have Potocani. That's just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you said Potocari or Potocani you're talking about the village that's not far away from Baljkovica, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on the map, it's a village called Potocani. It's a Muslim village near Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristic. I'd like you now, please, to have a look at 7D167. It's another page from the duty officer's notebook of the Zvornik Brigade. I wonder whether the B/C/S version could just be inched a little bit to the left so Mr. Ristic can read it. Could you read to yourself the large paragraph in the middle of that page, about the large group of armed and unarmed Turks?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm going to suggest to you, I want you to think about, that on the 15th of July, and that is a note from the 15th of July, the column at your rear, itself, was isolated and powerless. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which column do you have in mind? What did you have in mind specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have in mind the column that had come from Srebrenica, the people who are referred to as the large group of armed and unarmed Turks?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you agree that you were able at that stage to monitor their communications with the 2nd Corps who were in Nezuk at your front?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their arrival into the sector of Potocani, on the 15th, is something that we observed. We followed the situation, what we could see, and everything that had to do with the defence, and these activities, was done by Major Obrenovic, myself, and we were assisted by Captain Legenda. That was, roughly speaking, the defence of the command post, between our command and Potocani, we had the trenches that were dug out where our lines used to be earlier. Once they entered these trenches, they became a serious risk to the command post. They were assisted by the artillery support and they attacked the front end of defence in the area where we were supposed to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question in a way. They required assistance from the artillery support at your front to represent a danger to you, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I now want to move on to the 16th of July in the morning. There was further fighting on the 16th of July in the morning, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more intense. They came closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And during the course of that fighting, you captured a Muslim officer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He surrendered himself. He was approaching the headquarters with his hands up in the air. We didn't know who he was. Obrenovic said that we should let him approach. He approached. I was present when he entered the building where the headquarters was located. He had a wound on his neck, and there was blood coming out of his wound. There was a medical technician there from Vukovar who bandaged his wound because Major Obrenovic ordered that he be given medical assistance. We asked him if he could speak. He said he couldn't. And they brought him the paper and pencil and the first thing they asked him is why he had come, why he had surrendered. He said that he had come seeking to negotiate with someone because they wanted to surrender. Then they asked him how many of them there were. He wrote down that there were 5.000 civilians and 2.000 men fit for military service. Major Obrenovic conveyed that to Commander Pandurevic, who then said, "I will come down there to negotiate. Have him go back and come back with two women." Probably just to make it safer, because he said that he was an officer from a brigade from Srebrenica. However, once he left, having seen the disposition of our forces, having seen that we were out of ammunition because people were coming in asking for ammunition, and they attacked us. We assumed that we would be unable to continue defending ourselves after about one hour of combat. Thus, we pulled back towards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the place where the forces withdrew to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you repeat the name of where you drew back to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We withdrew towards the link of the 4th and 6th Battalion going from Baljkovacka Rijeka to Parlog. That was the positions of the 1st Company of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And about what time of the morning was it that this man was captured and interrogated and Dragan Obrenovic spoke to Vinko Pandurevic about him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we abandoned the headquarters at around 12.00. Most likely an hour prior to that, maybe even longer, because they kept him at the headquarters for some time but roughly that would be the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went back to his people, and this is when they started a more intense attack, both using artillery and infantry forces. They had mobile mortars, they came closer to the command, to the headquarters, so we were forced to leave the headquarters. Our plan was to join the lines, the front end of our defence. As we were pulling out and going along Baljkovacka Rijeka, we approached the trenches of the 1st Platoon of our 1st Company. It was then that on the radio we heard Commander Pandurevic informing us that he had agreed with Semso Muminovic to have a cease-fire, to stop shooting. He said that they would open a passage for the people to pass through without any hindrance, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you just explain to us how that was physically achieved? How was the corridor opened for these people to pass through?
